questions.question: Explain elastic rebound as the cause of earthquakes, distinguish the focus from the epicentre, and show why focus depth largely decides how destructive an event is.
questions.expected_answer: Plate movement loads the rock on either side of a fault with strain. The rock deforms elastically and stores the energy, like a drawn bow, while friction keeps the fault locked — sometimes for centuries. When the accumulated strain finally exceeds the rock's strength or the friction, the fault slips, both sides spring back toward their unstrained shape, and the stored energy escapes as seismic vibrations: elastic rebound. The focus, or hypocentre, is the point inside the crust where the rupture begins and energy is first released; the epicentre is the surface point vertically above it, where shaking is normally strongest. Focus depth is classed as shallow, from the surface to 70 kilometres, intermediate to 300, and deep to 700 kilometres. A shallow focus delivers energy to the surface almost undiluted, so the world's deadliest earthquakes are shallow; deep-focus events, which occur only along subduction zones, spend most of their energy on the way up. Aftershocks follow the main shock for days or months and often collapse structures already weakened.

questions.question: Describe the three types of seismic wave and explain how records from three seismic stations locate an epicentre.
questions.expected_answer: P-waves are compressional body waves that squeeze and stretch rock along the direction of travel; they are fastest — about six kilometres per second in the crust — arrive first, and cross solids, liquids and gases. S-waves are transverse body waves that whip rock from side to side; they travel at roughly half the P-wave speed, arrive second, and cannot cross liquids, which lack the rigidity to transmit sideways shear. Surface waves travel along the ground, arrive last, and have the largest amplitude, doing most damage. Because P and S waves leave the focus simultaneously but travel at different speeds, the interval between their arrivals at a station grows with distance, so the S-minus-P gap converts to a distance from the epicentre. One distance only places the epicentre somewhere on a circle around that station, and two circles still intersect twice; with three stations, the three circles intersect at a single point, which is the epicentre. This is triangulation, the standard method for locating every earthquake.

questions.question: One earthquake magnitude can produce vastly different death tolls in different countries. Using the 2010 Chile and Haiti earthquakes, explain the vulnerability factors involved and the preparedness measures that reduce losses.
questions.expected_answer: Deaths are governed by vulnerability rather than magnitude. In 2010 Chile's magnitude 8,8 earthquake released roughly five hundred times the energy of Haiti's magnitude 7,0, yet killed a tiny fraction of the people, because vulnerability differed. Building quality and enforcement matter most: shaking does not kill, failing structures do — Chile's enforced engineering codes kept collapse rare while Haiti's unreinforced concrete failed. Population density and urbanisation raise tolls where large or informal settlements lie near the epicentre; wealth and preparedness determine monitoring, drills, rescue capacity, hospitals and insurance; timing matters because night events catch people asleep indoors; and local ground matters because soft sediment amplifies shaking — liquefaction undermined suburbs of Christchurch in 2011 — while bedrock transmits less. Since prediction of dates remains impossible, preparedness works in three layers: engineering, including base isolation, cross-bracing, bedrock foundations and light roofs; planning, through zoning that keeps schools, hospitals and dense housing off faults and soft ground with inspected building codes; and people and systems — rehearsed drop-cover-hold drills, emergency supplies, family meeting points, early-warning networks giving seconds before the surface waves, and tsunami alerts for coasts.
